title: Orders With Names
statement:
List every order together with the name of the customer who placed it.

The `customers` table has one row per customer:

- `id`: the customer's id
- `name`: the customer's name
- `email`: their email address

The `orders` table has one row per order:

- `id`: the order's id
- `customer_id`: the `id` of the customer who placed it
- `amount`: what the order cost

Return one row per order with two columns, `order_id` (the order's `id`) and `customer` (the customer's `name`), sorted by `order_id`.

Expected output:

```text
 order_id |  customer
----------+-------------
     1001 | Omar Haddad
     1002 | Maya Lopez
     1003 | Grace Kim
     1004 | Omar Haddad
     1005 | Lucas Silva
     1006 | Maya Lopez
(6 rows)
```
setup:
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  name text NOT NULL,
  email text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (id),
  amount numeric(8, 2) NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO customers (id, name, email) VALUES
  (1, 'Maya Lopez', 'maya@example.com'),
  (2, 'Omar Haddad', 'omar@example.com'),
  (3, 'Grace Kim', 'grace@example.com'),
  (4, 'Lucas Silva', 'lucas@example.com');

INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, amount) VALUES
  (1001, 2, 42.00),
  (1002, 1, 18.50),
  (1003, 3, 99.99),
  (1004, 2, 7.25),
  (1005, 4, 63.10),
  (1006, 1, 25.00);

hints: Each order has a `customer_id`. Match it to the `id` in `customers` with `JOIN ... ON`.
Give the tables short aliases, like `orders AS o` and `customers AS c`, so you can say which `id` you mean.

sql.starter:
-- TODO: join customers so each order shows its customer's name
SELECT id AS order_id, customer_id AS customer
FROM orders
ORDER BY id;
sql.solution:
SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY o.id;
